title: Dilucidationes super methodo elegantissima, qua illustris de la Grange usus est in integranda aequatione differentiali dx/√X = dy/√Y

deep.reconstruction:
Problem: integrate the separated Riccati-type equation dx/X + dy/Y = 0, where X = a+2bx+cx² and Y = a+2by+cy². Euler adapts Lagrange's 'time' method, which Lagrange devised for dx/√X = dy/√Y with quartic X. Set dx/dt = X and dy/dt = −Y.

§17 (previous page): Euler forms (y dx + x dy)/dt = yX − xY and puts u = xy and q = x − y. Then du/dt = a(y−x) + cxy(x−y) = q(cu−a), because the 2b-terms cancel.

This page:
- Dividing by cu−a and multiplying by c gives c du/(dt(cu−a)) = cq. The left side is a logarithmic differential.

§18:
- Differentiate the defining equations with dt constant: ddx/(dt dx) = X' = 2b+2cx and ddy/(dt dy) = −Y' = −(2b+2cy).
- Their sum is X' − Y' = 2c(x−y) = 2cq.
- Subtract twice the previous relation: d(ln dx + ln dy − 2 ln(cu−a)) = 0.
- Hence dx·dy/(cu−a)² = C dt². Substituting dx = X dt and dy = −Y dt gives the first integral −XY/(cu−a)² = C, i.e. XY/(a−cxy)² = const.

§19: The integral is (a+2bx+cx²)(a+2by+cy²)/(a−cxy)² = C. Subtracting 1 gives [2ab(x+y) + ac(x+y)² + 4b²xy + 2bcxy(x+y)]/(a−cxy)² = C.

§20 begins the check with a=1, b=0, c=1. The equation becomes dx/(1+x²) + dy/(1+y²) = 0, whose known integral is arctan x + arctan y = arctan((x+y)/(1−xy)) = C. On the next page the formula gives ((x+y)/(1−xy))² = C, which agrees.

Modern view: Euler finds an algebraic first integral (invariant) of the flow by building an integrating factor from logarithmic derivatives. The relation is the addition law for the 'logarithm/arctangent' attached to a quadratic. It is the degree-2 analogue of the symmetric biquadratic relation behind Euler's addition theorem for elliptic integrals.
errors: No mathematical errors. du/dt = q(cu−a) is correct; X' − Y' = 2cq is correct. The expansion XY − (a−cxy)² = 2ab(x+y) + ac(x+y)² + 4b²xy + 2bcxy(x+y) checks term by term. The sign handling (−XY/(cu−a)² = C, then rewritten with (a−cxy)²) is harmless because C is arbitrary.
Minor point: the second differentiation tacitly assumes dt constant (ddt = 0), as in Lagrange's method. This is standard and implicit, not an error.

ideas.what: Extension of Lagrange's auxiliary-time method to dx/(a+2bx+cx²) + dy/(a+2by+cy²) = 0. The trick is to pass to u = xy and q = x−y, obtaining du/dt = q(cu−a).
ideas.modern_name: Construction of a first integral via logarithmic integrating factors (Darboux-type invariant)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler, in this paper (E506), as an extension of Lagrange (Misc. Taurinensia IV, 1766-69)
ideas.where_published: E506 itself (Acta Acad. Sci. Petrop. 1780, publ. 1783)

ideas.what: Algebraic integral XY/(a−cxy)² = C of the separated rational equation, i.e. the addition law for integrals of dx/(quadratic).
ideas.modern_name: Addition theorem for arctan/logarithm; degree-2 case of Euler's symmetric addition relation
ideas.where_published: Institutiones calculi integralis vol. I (E342), chapters on comparing transcendental quantities; the algebraic integration of separated equations (E251, E345 etc.) — exact location unsure

deep.surprise_reason: This is a clean, correct, well-known computation in a published and studied paper. Both the integral and the method extension are explicitly Euler's and documented, so nothing here appears to be missing from the record.
transcription_corrections: None significant. The page transcription matches the image ('C dt²' is printed with a superscript 2). On the previous page, 'aquationem' should read 'aequationem'.
